title: The Standard Discrete Distributions
summary: A small family of distributions accounts for most discrete models. For each we state the model, derive the PMF, and compute the mean and variance. We use only tools developed so far; where independence of random variables would give a shorter derivation,…

intro.x: A small family of distributions accounts for most discrete models. For each we state the model, derive the PMF, and compute the mean and variance. We use only tools developed so far; where independence of random variables would give a shorter derivation, we note it and give the proof in Chapter 6.

blocks.x: $X$ has the Bernoulli$(p)$ distribution if $\Prob(X=1)=p$ and $\Prob(X=0)=1-p=q$. This is the indicator of a “success” in one trial.
Its mean is $p$ and its variance is $pq$ (Chapter 4, indicators).
$X$ has the binomial$(n,p)$ distribution if
\Prob(X=k)=\binom nkp^kq^{n-k},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,n .
It is the number of successes in $n$ independent trials, each with success probability $p$ (Example 3.16).
The probabilities sum to $1$ by the binomial theorem: $\sum_k\binom nkp^kq^{n-k}=(p+q)^n=1$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Mean and variance of the binomial

blocks.x: If $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ then $\Exp[X]=np$ and $\Var(X)=npq$.
We use the identities $k\binom nk=n\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ and $k(k-1)\binom nk=n(n-1)\binom{n-2}{k-2}$, both immediate from the factorial formula. Then

\Exp[X]=\sum_{k=1}^nk\binom nkp^kq^{n-k}=np\sum_{k=1}^n\binom{n-1}{k-1}p^{k-1}q^{n-k}
=np\,(p+q)^{n-1}=np.
Similarly
\Exp[X(X-1)]=\sum_{k=2}^nk(k-1)\binom nkp^kq^{n-k}=n(n-1)p^2(p+q)^{n-2}=n(n-1)p^2.
Hence $\Exp[X^2]=\Exp[X(X-1)]+\Exp[X]=n(n-1)p^2+np$ and
\Var(X)=n(n-1)p^2+np-n^2p^2=np-np^2=npq.
(Probabilistic shortcut: $X$ is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables; linearity gives the mean at once and independence gives the variance, as shown in Chapter 6.)

The ratio $\dfrac{\Prob(X=k)}{\Prob(X=k-1)}=\dfrac{(n-k+1)p}{kq}$ exceeds $1$ iff $k<(n+1)p$. So the PMF increases up to $\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor$ and decreases afterwards; the mode is $\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor$ (with a tie at $k=(n+1)p$ when this is an integer).
The ratio is a direct computation from the PMF. The inequality $(n-k+1)p>kq$ rearranges to $(n+1)p>k(p+q)=k$.
$X$ has the geometric$(p)$ distribution, $0
\Prob(X=k)=q^{k-1}p,\qquad k=1,2,\dots
It is the number of independent trials up to and including the first success.
The total mass is $\sum_{k\ge1}q^{k-1}p=p/(1-q)=1$. The tail is $\Prob(X\ge k)=q^{k-1}$ (the first $k-1$ trials fail).
$\Exp[X]=1/p$ and $\Var(X)=q/p^2$.

By the tail-sum formula (Proposition 4.16(v)), $\Exp[X]=\sum_{k\ge1}q^{k-1}=1/(1-q)=1/p$. For the variance compute $\Exp[X(X-1)]=\sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)q^{k-1}p$. Differentiating the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}x^k=(1-x)^{-1}$ twice (valid for $\abs x<1$) gives $\sum_{k\ge2}k(k-1)x^{k-2}=2(1-x)^{-3}$. Hence
So $\Exp[X^2]=\frac{2q}{p^2}+\frac1p$ and $\Var(X)=\frac{2q}{p^2}+\frac1p-\frac1{p^2}=\frac{2q+p-1}{p^2}=\frac q{p^2}$.
If $X\sim\mathrm{Geom}(p)$ then for non-negative integers $m,n$,
\Prob(X>m+n\given X>m)=\Prob(X>n).
Conversely, if $X$ takes values in $\{1,2,\dots\}$, has $\Prob(X>n)>0$ for all $n$, and satisfies this identity, then $X$ is geometric.

We have $\Prob(X>n)=q^n$. Then $\Prob(X>m+n\given X>m)=q^{m+n}/q^m=q^n$. Conversely, let $G(n)=\Prob(X>n)$. The condition says $G(m+n)=G(m)G(n)$, so $G(n)=G(1)^n$ by induction. Setting $q=G(1)=\Prob(X>1)$ gives $\Prob(X>n)=q^n$ and so $\Prob(X=n)=q^{n-1}-q^n=q^{n-1}(1-q)$, the geometric PMF with $p=1-q$.
In words: the process “forgets” its past. If you have already failed $m$ times, the number of further trials is distributed as if you were starting over.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: two conventions for the geometric distribution

blocks.x: Some books define the geometric variable as the number of failures before the first success, taking values $0,1,2,\dots$ with mean $q/p$. Always check the convention. In this book geometric counts trials, starting at $1$.
$X$ has the negative binomial$(r,p)$ distribution if it is the trial number on which the $r$th success occurs:
\Prob(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^rq^{k-r},\qquad k=r,r+1,\dots

Derivation. The $r$th success is on trial $k$ exactly when trial $k$ is a success and exactly $r-1$ of the first $k-1$ trials are successes. The latter has probability $\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^{r-1}q^{k-r}$, and multiplying by the independent success probability $p$ on trial $k$ gives the formula. With $r=1$ we recover the geometric distribution.
If $X\sim\mathrm{NB}(r,p)$ then $\Exp[X]=r/p$.
Use $k\binom{k-1}{r-1}=r\binom kr$. Then

\Exp[X]=\sum_{k\ge r}k\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^rq^{k-r}
=\frac rp\sum_{k\ge r}\binom kr p^{r+1}q^{k-r}.

The terms in the last sum are $\Prob(Y=k+1)$ for $Y\sim\mathrm{NB}(r+1,p)$, since $\binom{(k+1)-1}{(r+1)-1}p^{r+1}q^{(k+1)-(r+1)}=\binom kr p^{r+1}q^{k-r}$. The PMF of $Y$ sums to $1$ over $k+1=r+1,r+2,\dots$, so the sum equals $1$.
(The mean $r/p$ is expected: waiting for $r$ successes is $r$ consecutive waits, each with mean $1/p$.)
$X$ has the Poisson$(\lambda)$ distribution, $\lambda>0$, if
\Prob(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots
Total mass: $\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!=e^{-\lambda}e^\lambda=1$ by the exponential series.
Let $X_n\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_n)$ with $np_n\to\lambda\in(0,\infty)$. Then for every fixed $k\ge0$,
\Prob(X_n=k)\longrightarrow e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}.
Write $\lambda_n=np_n\to\lambda$. Then

\Prob(X_n=k)=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}\,\frac{\lambda_n^k}{n^k}
\Bigl(1-\frac{\lambda_n}n\Bigr)^{n-k}.

As $n\to\infty$ with $k$ fixed: $\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^k}= \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-j/n)\to1$; $\lambda_n^k\to\lambda^k$; $(1-\lambda_n/n)^{-k}\to1$; and $(1-\lambda_n/n)^n\to e^{-\lambda}$. For the last limit, take logarithms: $n\ln(1-\lambda_n/n)=-\lambda_n+O(\lambda_n^2/n)\to-\lambda$, using $\ln(1-x)=-x+O(x^2)$ as $x\to0$. Multiplying the limits gives the claim.
If $X\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ then $\Exp[X]=\Var(X)=\lambda$.

$\Exp[X]=\sum_{k\ge1}k\,e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}=\lambda\sum_{k\ge1} e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}=\lambda$. Likewise $\Exp[X(X-1)]=\sum_{k\ge2}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{(k-2)!}=\lambda^2$, so $\Var(X)=\lambda^2+\lambda-\lambda^2=\lambda$.

The binomial limit explains the meaning: Poisson models the number of rare events among many opportunities, where each event is unlikely but the expected total $\lambda$ is moderate (misprints on a page, calls arriving at an exchange in a minute, radioactive decays). It is also consistent with the moments: the binomial has mean $np\to\lambda$ and variance $npq\to\lambda$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: how good is the Poisson approximation?

blocks.x: For $X=\sum_{i=1}^nI_i$ a sum of independent Bernoulli$(p_i)$ indicators with $\lambda=\sum p_i$, the distance between the law of $X$ and the Poisson$(\lambda)$ law (in total variation) is at most $\sum_ip_i^2$ (Le Cam’s inequality; we cite it without proof). The approximation is good when every individual $p_i$ is small, even if the $p_i$ differ. It can also be good under weak dependence (the Chen–Stein method), as in the birthday problem for matching pairs.

A book has $500$ pages and $400$ misprints, each independently on a uniformly random page. The number on a given page is $\mathrm{Bin}(400,1/500)$, with mean $0.8$. Poisson$(0.8)$ gives $\Prob(\text{no misprint on page 1})\approx e^{-0.8}\approx0.449$; the exact value is $(499/500)^{400}\approx0.4489$.
An urn contains $N$ balls, $K$ of them red. Draw $n$ balls without replacement. The number $X$ of red balls drawn has the hypergeometric distribution:
\Prob(X=k)=\frac{\binom Kk\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom Nn},

for integers $k$ with $\max(0,n-N+K)\le k\le\min(n,K)$. Counting argument: all $\binom Nn$ subsets of size $n$ are equally likely; those with exactly $k$ red balls are formed by choosing the red ones and the non-red ones separately. The probabilities sum to $1$ by Vandermonde’s identity (Theorem 1.16).
$\Exp[X]=n\dfrac KN$.

Number the draws $1,\dots,n$ and let $I_j$ indicate that draw $j$ is red. Then $X=\sum_jI_j$. By symmetry each draw is equally likely to be any of the $N$ balls, so $\Prob(I_j=1)=K/N$, even though the draws are dependent. Linearity of expectation gives $\Exp[X]=nK/N$.

The variance $n\frac KN\bigl(1-\frac KN\bigr)\frac{N-n}{N-1}$ is derived in Example 6.14 of the next chapter. Notice that it is the binomial variance (drawing with replacement, $p=K/N$) times the finite population correction $\frac{N-n}{N-1}$.
Let $N\to\infty$ with $K/N\to p\in(0,1)$ and $n$ fixed. Then the hypergeometric PMF converges to the Bin$(n,p)$ PMF.

Write $\Prob(X=k)=\binom nk\dfrac{K(K-1)\cdots(K-k+1)\cdot(N-K)\cdots(N-K-n+k+1)} {N(N-1)\cdots(N-n+1)}$ (counting ordered sequences with a specified pattern of red and non-red positions, times the $\binom nk$ patterns). The numerator has $k$ factors each $\sim pN$ and $n-k$ factors each $\sim(1-p)N$; the denominator has $n$ factors each $\sim N$. Hence the ratio tends to $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$.
The negative binomial variance $rq/p^2$ is verified in Chapter 6 (sum of $r$ independent geometrics).

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: recognising the distribution from the story

blocks.x: Most exam problems say which distribution to use if you identify the story: fixed number of independent trials, count successes: binomial; trials until first success: geometric; trials until $r$th success: negative binomial; sampling without replacement from a finite population, count a type: hypergeometric; rare events in a large number of opportunities: Poisson. Always state which assumption (independence, constant $p$) justifies the choice.
A fair coin is tossed $10$ times. Find the probabilities of exactly $5$ heads, at least $8$ heads, and the most likely number of heads.
A basketball player makes each free throw with probability $0.7$, independently. What is the probability the first miss occurs on the fourth shot? The expected number of shots until the first miss?
Prove: if $X\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, then $\Prob(X=k+1)/\Prob(X=k)= \lambda/(k+1)$, and deduce the mode is $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor$.
A call centre receives on average $3$ calls per minute (Poisson). Find the probability of no calls in a given minute, and of more than $5$ calls.

Banach’s matchbox: a person has two boxes with $n$ matches each, picking a box at random for each use. When a box is found empty, the other contains $k$ matches. Show the probability is $\binom{2n-k}{n}2^{-(2n-k)}$. (Count the draws carefully; there are two symmetric cases.)
Show $\Exp[1/(1+X)]=\frac{1-q^{n+1}}{(n+1)p}$ for $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$.
In a lottery $6$ numbers are drawn from $49$. Find the probability that a ticket with $6$ chosen numbers matches exactly $3$.
Prove the memoryless property for the geometric distribution in the form $\Exp[X-m\given X>m]=\Exp[X]$.

(Challenge) Prove the Poisson limit theorem (Theorem 5.11) for hypergeometric variables: if $N\to\infty$, $K\to\infty$, $n\to\infty$ with $nK/N\to\lambda$ and $n/N\to0$, then the hypergeometric PMF converges to Poisson.
